title: How an accounting firm should write an about page
metaTitle: Accounting firm about page that names people
excerpt: An accounting firm about page should name who does the work and why a founder should care. Keep the origin story only if it changes the decision to book.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back, objects identified by what they are rather than by a slogan.
caption: Two views of the same object, face and back, so you can tell what it is. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an accountant's biography include?
faqs.answer: Include the name, the role, the jobs they do, and the kinds of companies they do them for. Say who signs the work if that person is different from the one who closes the month. Four to six specific sentences are enough. A list of every industry they have touched hides the fit.

faqs.question: Do accounting firm about pages need a founding story?
faqs.answer: Only when the story changes whether this founder should book a call. A boundary, such as working only with owner-led companies, can lead. A garage story or a claim of excellence can sit lower or leave. The founder came to find a person, not a memoir.

faqs.question: Where should licenses appear?
faqs.answer: Put the registration beside the person who holds it, in the words your regulator uses. Founders look for who signs. A PDF in the footer is easy to miss, and a badge with no name does not answer the question.

markdown:
An accounting firm about page is proof that people stand behind the offer. Name who does the work, and say why a founder who needs a calm expert should care. Skip the origin myth unless that story changes the decision to book a call. A skyline and the word excellence do not identify the person who will explain a number.

Google's helpful-content guidance treats "who" as part of trust. It asks whether a visitor can tell who created the page, and it gives more weight to experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trust when the topic can affect financial stability. Handing someone your books is that kind of decision. A glass tower and a founding year do not answer who will close the month.

## The person is the proof

The founder may already know the job, monthly books, a cleanup, a return. The about page answers who will do it, and why that person fits a company like theirs.

Lead with the people who touch the work, not with a group photo on a roof. For each person, give the name, the role, the jobs they actually do, and the kinds of companies they do them for. Those four facts are the proof. A line about being passionate about excellence is not.

Separate the roles in plain language. Who talks to the founder. Who closes the ledger. Who reviews and signs. A founder looking for calm wants to know they will not explain the business to a new stranger every month. If a bookkeeper does the close and a licensed reviewer signs the return, say both. Hiding the distinction creates the surprise the pricing page tried to prevent.

Google's title-link guidance warns against vague titles such as "Profile" for a specific person. "Jonah Ellison, monthly closes for owner-led studios" is a heading a founder can use. "Our people" still needs a click. Put the name and the work in the heading.

## Why this founder should care

The reason to care is the overlap between their company and this person's work. "He closes the books for studios and agencies that invoice by project, and he will tell you when a number is a timing issue rather than a crisis." That sentence helps a founder. A paragraph about loving spreadsheets since school does not.

Keep the reason tied to the kind of company. Product companies with a first finance hire still missing. Clinics with practitioner billings. Shops with stock. If different people lead different kinds, say so. A founder should be able to request that person, or at least that pod, when they book.

Add the practical overlaps. Which ledgers they work in. Whether they meet by video or in the office. How questions usually get answered, if that is stable. Whether they have done cleanups before a lender pack, if that is a job you offer. These are reasons to book. They are also reasons to look elsewhere, which is a fair outcome.

Leave awards in a quiet list, current and real. They do not replace the sentence about the work. A badge next to an empty bio is the same costume as a skyline.

Licenses and registrations belong beside the person who holds them, in the words your regulator uses. Founders who have been burned look for who signs. Put that fact where the name is, not in a PDF three clicks down.

## The origin myth test

Delete the firm story and ask whether a founder would still know whether to book. If yes, the story can sit low or leave.

"We opened in 2009 to bring excellence to small business" does not change a booking. "We only work with owner-led companies, and we still decline listed groups" does. The second sentence is a boundary that happens to be historical. Lead with the boundary. The year is optional.

A long tale about a garage, a first client who paid in trade, or a view from the old office reassures the founders of the firm. The founder reading the page has a ledger question. Nielsen Norman Group's finding that people read about a quarter of the text is a reason to spend that quarter on names, roles, and company types.

If the story is the only place you say who the firm is for, move that fact into the first screen and shorten the story to a sentence under the people. Do not make them earn the point of the page by reading a memoir.

## What a short biography should hold

Four to six sentences are enough when they are specific.

Name and role. The jobs, in founder language. The kinds of companies. One concrete detail of how they work, such as writing the question back in a shared note rather than a slide. What they sign, if they sign. How to book time with the firm and mention them.

Mention the companies only as types. Do not drop client names into a bio to borrow their reputation unless you have permission and the mention is still true. A founder can feel the difference between a type they recognize and a logo wall.

Skip the list of every industry they have ever invoiced. It recreates the vague grid. Match the bio to the services you feature. If the services page says you close the month for studios, the about page should show the person who does that close.

Keep the tone even. Superlatives about being the city's leading advisor are hard to trust and awkward to maintain. A description of the work is stronger. Write in the third person if several people share the page, so the voice stays steady. Calm is a tone you can edit for. It shows up as fewer adjectives and clearer nouns. Read the bio aloud. If you run out of breath before the job appears, the adjectives are still in the way.

If someone leaves, take them off the page that week. An about page that still offers a call with a person who is gone is a trust failure on a financial site. Update the who-signs line the same day if the signer changed. A founder should not meet a different reviewer than the page named. That is not a branding task for later.

## Photographs should identify

Use a photograph in which the person is recognizable, in the room where they work if you can. A founder on a video call should see the same human. A skyline does not identify an accountant. A watch on a marble desk does not either.

Match the picture to the sentence. If the bio says she closes the books, a photo at a laptop with a normal screen, locked so no client data shows, is enough. Tell people to clear the screen before the shutter. A leaked dashboard is not authenticity.

Alt text should describe the person and the setting. "Jonah Ellison at a wooden desk with a laptop, the screen turned away." Captions can say the job. "Closes the month for owner-led studios." Do not caption a portrait with excellence.

If someone declines a photo, publish the name and the work anyway. A missing face is honest. A stock face is not. Say that the first call is by video so the founder knows they will meet a real person then.

## How the page ends

Close on the booking. The founder has just read who does the work. Let them book a call without hunting. One line on what to have in mind: entity, ledger, the question. Repeat that the call is a fit check, not a completed return.

Link the two or three services those people deliver, so the about page and the services page agree. A bio that promises investor diligence, while the services page only offers annual returns, is a contradiction a careful founder will notice and should.

Read the top of the page for ten seconds. Who works here, and for what kind of company? If the answer is a skyline, rewrite the opening. Jakob Nielsen's rule is that the value has to be clear within 10 seconds if you want the longer visit. On this page the value is a person matched to a company type.

## When the story belongs first

Keep history at the top only when it is the boundary. "We work with independent clinics and we do not take hospitals" can be the first sentence if it is true and if it is why the firm exists. Follow it with the people who do that work now. A story about the past, with the current accountants postponed, asks the founder to care about you before they know you can help.

The next thing they need, once they trust a name, is a pattern of a decision. A face is not a case. Read [how a proof page shows the constraint and the decision](/blog/proof-pages-for-an-accounting-firm) before you publish a client result you are not allowed to show.

When you want help judging whether the people are as clear as the offer, [book an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the bios as they read with the photographs covered.
